summary: How many payments per second the service sustains on 2 CPUs and 3 GB, and how each change got it there. Stages 1–7 were measured from their own commits in one run, stage 8 in a second run on the same machine; a step holds with p95 under 200 ms.
conditions: app 1 CPU, Postgres 1 CPU; mains power; stages 1–7 on 2026-10-17/18, stage 8 on 2026-10-18

stages.name: 1. Start: blocking JDBC
stages.change: Stored running balances; six ways of keeping balances compared

stages.name: 2. Group commit
stages.change: BATCHED: one writer commits queued requests together; STORED unchanged

stages.name: 3. Database work off Ktor's 3 request threads
stages.change: Profiling: blocking JDBC on 3 request threads capped concurrency; moved to the IO dispatcher

stages.name: 4. No deferred balance trigger
stages.change: The trigger re-checked each entry 5 times per capture at commit; the check stays in code

stages.name: 5. await in the batch commit
stages.change: A request waiting for its batch suspends instead of holding a thread; STORED unchanged

stages.name: 6. Batched inserts in the driver
stages.change: reWriteBatchedInserts: a capture's 4 postings go as one INSERT

stages.name: 7. JDBC through table objects
stages.change: Code refactor, no performance intent; batches of 1000 with a 50 ms wait tried: 600–700 rps, p95 106 ms at 300/s

stages.name: 8. Set-based batch writes
stages.change: The batch writer was busy 92% at 0.85 ms per capture, statement by statement; a batch's captures are now one multi-row INSERT per table, responses from memory

start.note: stage 1, commit 0ffcf3f: all capped near 300 rps by the 3 request threads found in stage 3

methods.name: Snapshot + tail
methods.read: snapshot + postings since the last refresh
